study_identification_part.si4_title: Lifespan Normative Models of White Matter Fractional Anisotropy: Applications to Early Psychosis

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To develop large-scale normative models of white matter fractional anisotropy (FA) across the lifespan using data from over 25,000 healthy individuals, and to apply these models to understand heterogeneity in white matter FA in early psychosis.

rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.answer: FSL-based pipelines; HCP-pipeline (for HCP datasets); DTIfit (DTI modeling); TBSS (Tract-Based Spatial Statistics); JHU atlas segmentation
rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.reason: The paper provides detailed description of the preprocessing pipeline, including specific software packages and processing steps. FSL-based pipelines were used harmoniously across all datasets.
rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: Methods: 'The processing of these datasets followed harmonized FSL-based pipelines, summarized in Figure 1A. Initially, pre-processing was performed: B0 intensity normalization, correction for EPI distortions, eddy-current-induced and movement corrections. These corrections were executed using the HCP-pipeline [42] for the HCP datasets while the UKB dataset was already processed according to the UKB documentation [43]. Subsequently, we estimated the DTI model using DTIfit on the lowest shell value in order to extract the fractional anisotropy (FA) values. Following this, we ran Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS) [44] on the FA images which included registration to a standard space (FMRIB58_FA), projection of each individual's FA image to the standard space skeletonized image (threshold at 0.2) to generate skeletonized FA images for each individual in the same space. Finally, segmentation was conducted using the Johns Hopkins University (JHU) atlas [45].'

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Multi-view sparse canonical correlation analysis (msCCA) with stability selection was used to map associations between three views of data: (1) PANSS symptom domains (positive, negative, cognitive/disorganized, and total PANSS), (2) FA deviations across 48 white matter tracts, and (3) structural deviations (cortical thickness and subcortical volumes from previously published normative models). The analysis used L1-norm sparsity regularization (90% of PANSS features, 20% of FA features, 20% of structural features selected). Stability selection was performed over 1000 random 70-30 train-test splits, with features selected in >80% of splits considered stable. Permutation testing (1000 permutations) was used to assess significance of test canonical correlations. For group-level analyses, t-tests with FDR correction were used to assess mean differences in deviations between patients and controls. Mann-Whitney U tests with FDR correction were used to test for differences in proportion of extreme deviations between groups.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Large-scale normative models of white matter FA revealed extensive inter-individual heterogeneity in early psychosis, with patients showing significantly more extreme deviations (both positive and negative) than controls despite no significant group-level mean differences; multivariate analysis identified the right uncinate fasciculus and bilateral thalamus as key regions associated with symptom severity.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The study developed normative models with good fit quality (mean EV=0.37±0.10, skewness=-0.09±0.12, kurtosis=0.42±0.27) capturing lifespan trajectories across 48 white matter tracts. In the HCP-EP cohort, no significant mean differences in FA deviations survived FDR correction between patients and controls, although nominally significant effects were found in the fornix and stria terminalis bilaterally. However, individuals with early psychosis showed significantly greater proportions of both extreme positive (Mann-Whitney U=1403.0, p=0.0036) and extreme negative (U=1517.0, p=0.0016) z-score deviations (|Z|>2.6) compared to controls, with negative deviations being particularly pronounced. The multivariate msCCA analysis yielded a significant test canonical correlation of r=0.25 (p=0.003) for the first component, driven primarily by cognitive symptoms and total PANSS scores. Stability selection (threshold >0.8) identified FA in the right uncinate fasciculus (positive weight) and bilateral thalamic volumes (negative weights) as the most stable predictors of symptom severity. The model showed good predictive performance for associations between symptoms and both FA deviations and structural deviations, but deliberately not between diffusion and structural measures to avoid learning trivial correlations.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The authors released all normative models freely to the community via the PCN toolkit portal (https://github.com/ramonacirstian/fa_normative_modeling) and their established open-source software platforms. Models are available both with and without race as a covariate, allowing researchers to choose which is most appropriate for their needs. The paper demonstrates the value of normative models for multimodal data fusion. Transfer learning was successfully used to adapt the models to a new clinical site (HCP-EP) using only half of the available controls (N=27-28) for calibration. The approach captures heterogeneity not detected by traditional case-control analyses, potentially enabling future cohort stratification for precision medicine applications. The authors note this is the first comprehensive normative model for diffusion-weighted imaging measures at this scale and plan to augment with additional metrics (MD, NODDI) in future work.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Age distribution is skewed with limited data at extremes (ages 5-8 and >85 years), potentially limiting generalizability for younger children and oldest adults. Variability due to socioeconomic background was not explored. Self-reported race is an imperfect proxy for ethnicity, and the datasets are biased toward WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) populations. While site-specific differences were accounted for via fixed effects and transfer learning, more flexible modeling approaches may be needed to fully address ethnic/racial diversity. The study focused only on FA; other diffusion metrics (MD, NODDI) were not modeled. Visual inspection, mentioned as the gold standard for diffusion QC, was not explicitly stated as performed. The HCP-EP sample size is moderate for the multivariate clinical analyses.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a preprint posted on bioRxiv and has not yet undergone peer review, as indicated by the absence of a DOI with '10.' prefix. The paper represents the first large-scale normative modeling effort for diffusion MRI data, specifically FA, addressing a significant gap in the field. The authors emphasize several technical challenges that delayed normative modeling of diffusion data: (1) later development timeline compared to sMRI/fMRI, (2) computational intensity of processing, (3) reliance on visual QC as gold standard, (4) high sensitivity to scanner/vendor/sequence parameters. The study specifically chose to use datasets with closely harmonized protocols (all HCP datasets and UK Biobank use multi-shell diffusion with similar FSL-based processing) to maximize data quality and minimize residual site effects. The paper includes comprehensive supplementary materials showing: model fit statistics (Fig S1), complete centile plots for all 48 tracts (Fig S2), models without race covariate (Fig S3), detailed overlap of extreme deviations (Fig S4), demographic tables for training data (Table S1) and HCP-EP data (Table S2). Race/ethnicity demographics show substantial variation across datasets: UK Biobank is 96.90% White, while HCP datasets show more diversity (e.g., HCPA: 69.90% White, 14.95% Black, 7.96% Asian). The authors specifically address racial fairness by providing models both with and without race, and acknowledge ongoing work on this topic. Transfer learning approach allows efficient adaptation to new sites with small calibration samples. The msCCA analysis deliberately avoids optimizing correlations between different neuroimaging modalities to prevent learning trivial associations and focuses on shared variance with symptoms. Future directions include adding more diffusion metrics (MD, NODDI models), increasing data density at age extremes, and exploring socioeconomic covariates.
